name: Trigeminal trophic syndrome
aliases: trophic ulceration of the nasal ala

clinicalPearls: Characterised by a triad of trigeminal sensory loss, facial paraesthesia (often a crawling or itching dysaesthesia), and a self-induced ulcer, classically of the nasal ala
The crescentic ulcer typically spares the nasal tip because the tip is supplied by a different sensory branch, an important diagnostic clue
It follows damage to the trigeminal nerve or its ganglion, commonly after trigeminal ablative procedures for neuralgia, stroke, herpes zoster, or tumour
The ulceration is caused by repetitive self-manipulation (rubbing, picking, scratching) of anaesthetic and paraesthetic skin rather than by primary tissue breakdown
There may be a long latency, from months to years, between the nerve injury and the appearance of the ulcer
Diagnosis is clinical but requires biopsy and investigation to exclude malignancy, infection, and vasculitis, which can mimic it

Treatment centres on protecting the area and interrupting the itch-scratch cycle (barriers, behavioural measures, and neuropathic agents such as carbamazepine); surgical repair fails unless self-manipulation is stopped
reference.pathophysiology: Trigeminal trophic syndrome develops after injury to the trigeminal nerve, ganglion, or its central connections, producing sensory loss and abnormal paraesthetic sensations in the affected dermatome. The disordered sensation drives compulsive rubbing, picking, and scratching of the numb skin, and this repetitive self-inflicted trauma to tissue that lacks protective sensation produces a chronic, painless ulcer, most often on the ala of the nose. Impaired trophic and sensory function of the denervated skin contributes to poor healing, but the primary driver is mechanical self-manipulation rather than an intrinsic ischaemic or infective process. Characteristic sparing of the nasal tip reflects its innervation by a separate nerve branch.
additionalDifferentials: Basal cell or squamous cell carcinoma of the nose
Cutaneous infection (including mucormycosis and atypical mycobacteria)
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis and other vasculitides
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy of the ulcer edge to exclude malignancy and specific infection
Microbiological cultures including fungal and mycobacterial studies
MRI or CT of the brain and skull base to identify the underlying trigeminal lesion
Vasculitis screen including ANCA where relevant
Detailed sensory examination of the trigeminal territory
Review of prior trigeminal procedures, zoster, or stroke history
redFlags: An indurated or non-healing ulcer suggesting malignancy requiring biopsy
Rapidly progressive necrosis raising concern for invasive fungal infection
A new intracranial lesion accounting for the trigeminal injury
reference.prognosis: The ulcer is chronic and notoriously difficult to heal because it depends on stopping self-manipulation of insensate skin; with effective protection and behavioural interruption of the itch-scratch cycle healing can occur, but recurrence is common and reconstructive surgery fails if manipulation continues.
pitfalls: Mistaking the ulcer for a skin malignancy or infection, or vice versa, without biopsy
Attempting surgical reconstruction without first controlling the self-manipulation
Failing to recognise nasal tip sparing as a diagnostic clue
Overlooking the often long latency between nerve injury and ulceration
Not addressing the underlying trigeminal lesion or the paraesthesia driving the behaviour
references: Cummings Otolaryngology: Head and Neck Surgery
management: Interrupt the self-manipulation that drives the ulcer, using behavioural modification, physical barriers, occlusive dressings and protective devices to break the itch-scratch-pick cycle in the anaesthetic skin
Provide meticulous wound care with dressings and treat secondary bacterial infection with appropriate antimicrobials

Control the neuropathic dysaesthesia with agents such as carbamazepine, gabapentin, pregabalin or amitriptyline, and consider an antipsychotic such as pimozide when a compulsive picking element predominates
Exclude and treat mimics by biopsy to rule out malignancy, deep infection and vasculitis before attributing the ulcer to the syndrome
Identify and address the underlying trigeminal lesion, whether post-ablative, post-herpetic, vascular or neoplastic
Defer reconstructive surgery until self-manipulation is reliably controlled, as flaps and grafts fail if picking continues, and consider innervated flaps when repair is undertaken
Manage jointly across dermatology, neurology, plastic surgery and psychology or psychiatry
